story.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings

facts.text: Fiona Fung, the engineering leader of Anthropic's Claude Code and Cowork teams, said in a recent episode of Lenny's Podcast that agentic AI use in the workplace has increased so much it was making employees' work more solitary, pushing the company to intervene with other team-building activities.
Anthropic began implementing hackathons "just to make sure we're interacting together as a team," as well as pair programming lunches for employees to share how they're using Claude Code, Fung said.
The report also published comments from employees who said Claude has augmented their work and left humans in the driver's seat of selecting the direction for models to move.
Anthropic touted Claude's ability to ship more than 800 application programming interface (API) error fixes in April, a task the company said would have taken a human four years to complete.

"Where pairing was once about working through a tough problem together, it's now increasingly about seeing how a colleague uses these new tools and systems differently than you might, so even as more of the work shifts toward collaborating with agents, engineers keep learning from one another.
Anthropic has explored this tension in its own employees.
One worker expressed concern with the limitation of their own role in developing this technology.

The introduction of AI may complicate morale concerns, particularly because some of AI's greatest stalwarts—the engineers designing and training it—may be experiencing misgivings about the technology's advancements.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Anthropic's AI agents are now working six times as many hours as the employees directing them, while the share of junior workers among new technical hires has plunged from 27% to 9% — offering an early glimpse of how AI could reshape white-collar hiring, productivity and the structure of work.
Anthropic's agent data shows how deeply AI has penetrated its operations.
In March 2026, autonomous and interactive agent work hours surpassed human work hours for the first time.
The findings come from Anthropic 's new report, which draws on internal employment, AI-use, output, survey, communication, calendar and hiring data, alongside interviews with 17 employees.
A study following 192 engineers who adopted coding agents and 74 who did not found that the amount of code added rose sharply after adoption.
Anthropic cautioned that more code does not automatically mean better code or greater business impact, but said it found no difference in certain measures of code subsequently removed or reverted.
The company found that even non-technical employees generate enough AI output to require more than half a working week to read everything.
As a result, workers are increasingly doing what Anthropic calls "meta-work", building tools to monitor agents, writing instructions, creating dashboards and reviewing one agent's work with another.
The second Anthropic study shows why its employees may see this transformation differently from the wider public.
On average, Anthropic staff expect AI to perform 75% of their current work by 2030, compared with 28% among U.S. workers.
At the same time, technical departments accounted for 56% of Anthropic's workforce, down from 61% a year earlier.
Technical hiring continued to rise in absolute numbers, but sales, finance and recruiting grew faster.
The biggest employment shift is happening at the entry level.
Job postings for junior roles also declined sharply from December 2025.
Yet Anthropic employees do not expect automation to mean the company stops hiring.
Ninety-five percent expect Anthropic's headcount to grow over the next 12 months, with the median employee expecting 66% growth.
Anthropic stresses these are employees' personal expectations, not company plans.

Anthropic said interactive Claude sessions spend around 80% of their time waiting for human input, meaning the agents themselves are often ready to continue while employees become the limiting factor.

Anthropic said engineers' code commits rose to five times their velocity six months earlier, while lawyers processed more contracts, accounts-payable workers handled more invoices and salespeople closed more deals.

Weâ€™re publishing this research because Anthropic runs roughly a year and a half ahead of the economy on AI adoption, so what happens at Anthropic could be a leading indicator for the broader world.And we hope that it gives policymakers, researchers, and workers lead time to prepare for the economic impacts of the future â€“ and take steps now to make sure everyone benefits from AI.
The shift began as teams increasingly found that Claude could handle work previously assigned to junior technical staff, including writing code and finding bugs.
"The thing that raised eyebrows was the uplift for performance engineers in particular and it basically overnight changed what we were looking for," Anthropic quoted one employee as saying.
As Anthropic's researchers put it, "Employees increasingly see their work as managing teams of Claudes," while human attention and judgment remain the bottlenecks the system struggles to overcome.
The AI-driven productivity surge has created an unexpected constraint -- humans cannot keep up with the work their agents generate.
The change is also reshaping what Anthropic wants from new hires.
Hiring managers increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment rather than narrow technical expertise and implementation skills.
